title: Globalisation: Developed and Developing Responses

cards.h: A force that everyone argues about
cards.b:
Globalisation is the process by which economies, societies and politics become more closely linked across borders. Trade, finance, technology, ideas and people all move faster and farther than before.

It is one of the most-asked topics in Paper II. The question is nearly always the same: does globalisation help or hurt? And for whom: developed states, developing states, or both?

The syllabus asks you to compare developed and developing responses. The best answers do three things: define the term with a scholar, show the debate (hyperglobalists, sceptics, transformationalists), and give a balanced verdict with Indian examples.

The topic has also changed fast. In 2025-26 the US raised tariffs sharply, the Supreme Court struck down part of them, and talk of "deglobalisation" grew. Your answer should show you know the story did not end in 2008.

Anthony Giddens, in The Consequences of Modernity (1990), described it as the intensification of worldwide social relations that link distant places, so that local events are shaped by events far away.

David Held, Anthony McGrew, David Goldblatt and Jonathan Perraton, Global Transformations (1999), defined it as growth in the extent, intensity, speed and impact of global connections.

Its dimensions

  • Economic: trade, investment, multinational firms, global finance, supply chains.
  • Political: rise of international organisations and global rules (WTO, IMF, UN), and a debate on state sovereignty.
  • Cultural: global media, brands, language, migration.
  • Technological: internet, containers, digital platforms and, today, AI.
  • Ecological and health: climate change, pandemics.

Marshall McLuhan's "global village" (1962) is the early image. Roland Robertson (Globalization, 1992) added glocalisation: global things adapt to local settings.

Held and McGrew's work is the source of this three-way split.

Hyperglobalists see a new age where the nation-state is obsolete. Kenichi Ohmae, The Borderless World (1990) and The End of the Nation State (1995). Thomas Friedman, The Lexus and the Olive Tree (1999) and The World Is Flat (2005).

Sceptics say integration was as high before 1914 and is mostly regional. Paul Hirst and Grahame Thompson, Globalization in Question (1996).

Transformationalists say globalisation is real but is reshaping, not ending, state power.

cards.h: The case for: gains from openness
cards.b:
Supporters point to evidence.

  • Jagdish Bhagwati, In Defense of Globalization (2004): trade and open markets lift incomes and cut poverty, and globalisation has a "human face" when combined with good policy.
  • Friedman: countries must wear a "Golden Straitjacket", meaning free-market rules that reward discipline and punish bad policy.
  • East Asia (South Korea, Taiwan, then China) grew fast through exports. Extreme poverty worldwide fell sharply from 1990.

The Washington Consensus

The term was coined by John Williamson in 1989 for ten policies: fiscal discipline, trade liberalisation, privatisation, deregulation, openness to FDI and others. The IMF and World Bank used them as conditions for loans (structural adjustment programmes) in the 1980s-90s. The WTO was set up in 1995 to lock in the rules.

China joined the WTO in December 2001 and became the "factory of the world".

cards.h: The case against: costs and discontents
cards.b:
• Joseph Stiglitz, Globalization and Its Discontents (2002): IMF policies and the way markets were opened hurt poor countries. He cites the 1997 Asian crisis.
  • Dani Rodrik, The Globalization Paradox (2011): the trilemma. You cannot have deep global integration, national sovereignty and democratic politics together. Pick two.
  • Dependency and world-system writers (Amin, Wallerstein): globalisation deepens core-periphery inequality.
  • Inequality. Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2013 in French; English 2014) documents rising wealth concentration. The "elephant curve" (Lakner and Milanovic, 2013; Milanovic's Global Inequality, 2016) suggests the lower middle class in rich countries gained little.
  • Environment and culture. Race-to-the-bottom worries, McDonaldisation (George Ritzer, 1993) and Benjamin Barber's Jihad vs. McWorld (1995).
  • State retreat. Susan Strange, The Retreat of the State (1996).

Rich states wrote the rules and gained, but not evenly inside each country.

  • Early response: push free trade and capital mobility. The US, EU and Japan shaped GATT and the WTO. They kept protection in sensitive areas, such as farm subsidies.
  • Costs at home. Factory jobs moved to Asia. The 2008 financial crisis spread through global banks and hurt many.
  • Backlash. Brexit (the vote in June 2016, exit on 31 January 2020), the 2016 US election, and the rise of populist parties. The slogan became "take back control".
  • New tools. Industrial policy, such as the US CHIPS Act and Inflation Reduction Act (2022), "friend-shoring", export controls on technology, and sanctions after Russia's invasion of Ukraine (2022).
  • Tariffs. In 2025 the US raised tariffs sharply. In February 2026 the US Supreme Court ruled in Learning Resources v. Trump that the emergency law (IEEPA) did not allow tariffs. The administration then used other laws, such as Section 122 and Section 301.

The paradox: the main architect of globalisation is now its biggest doubter.

There is no single "developing world" response.

East Asia: managed openness

South Korea and Taiwan used a developmental state: subsidies, export targets and protection of young industries, then opened up. China did similarly after 1978, with special economic zones.

Latin America and Africa: hard lessons

The 1980s debt crisis brought IMF programmes and austerity. Many countries became more reliant on raw-material exports. The 1990s brought mixed results.

Collective bargaining

Developing countries formed the G-77 (1964) and pressed for NIEO. In the WTO, they formed blocs like the G-20 on agriculture at Cancun (2003) to resist farm subsidies. BRICS and the New Development Bank (2014) are newer efforts.

Common features: concern for policy space, food security, technology transfer and fair rules. Today many ask for reform of the IMF quota system and debt relief, and for climate finance.

Commentators speak of slowbalisation: trade grew slower than GDP after 2008, though digital flows kept rising. The COVID-19 pandemic (2020) exposed fragile supply chains. War in Ukraine and tension in West Asia added shocks.

The WTO's March 2026 outlook put world merchandise trade growth for 2026 at about 1.9 percent, down from about 4.6 percent in 2025, a year boosted by importers rushing ahead of higher tariffs.

The multilateral system is under strain. At the WTO's 14th ministerial conference in Yaounde (March 2026), members failed to agree on extending the moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions, and the Appellate Body remained unrestored.

India's path shows a late-but-strong embrace.

  • 1991 crisis. A balance-of-payments emergency, with foreign exchange reserves covering only a few weeks of imports. Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh began LPG reforms (liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation). In July 1991 the rupee was devalued, industrial licensing was largely scrapped, and FDI rules were eased.
  • Results. A services and IT boom, higher growth, and a larger middle class. India was a founder-member of the WTO (1995).
  • Worries. Farm distress, jobs, jobless growth, and inequality.
  • Stance at the WTO. India defends farm subsidies and public stockholding for food security, as a developing-country voice.
  • New turn. "Make in India" (2014), Atmanirbhar Bharat (2020) and PLI schemes aim at manufacturing. At the same time India signs trade pacts. The India-UK CETA came into force on 15 July 2026, the India-EU FTA was concluded in January 2026, and India and the US announced an interim trade framework in February 2026, after tariffs on Indian goods had risen to 50% in 2025. Check the latest status before quoting rates.

"Globalisation has strengthened rather than weakened the nation-state." Discuss.
"Examine the responses of developed and developing countries to globalisation."
"Is the world moving towards deglobalisation? Comment."
"Discuss the impact of globalisation on developing countries with special reference to India."

Structure: define (Giddens, Held), list dimensions. Present the three schools in a box. Give gains (Bhagwati) and costs (Stiglitz, Rodrik's trilemma, Piketty). Separate developed and developing responses with 3 points each, including backlash, tariffs, East Asian model and G-77. Add the current picture: slowbalisation, 2025-26 tariffs, WTO MC14. End with India: 1991, WTO stance, Atmanirbhar Bharat plus FTAs.

Finish with a balanced judgement: globalisation is being reshaped, not reversed.

quiz.q: The three-way division into hyperglobalists, sceptics and transformationalists comes from:
Globalization in Question (1996) by Hirst and Thompson belongs to which school?
quiz.w: They argued that integration was not unprecedented and states remained central.

quiz.q: Dani Rodrik's trilemma says you cannot have all three of:
o: Hyperglobalisation, national sovereignty and democratic politics
Free speech, free press and free markets
quiz.w: You can pick only two of the three.

quiz.q: The term 'Washington Consensus' was coined by:
Joseph Stiglitz's Globalization and Its Discontents (2002) mainly criticises:
o: IMF policies and the manner of liberalisation
quiz.w: He argued IMF policies hurt developing countries, citing the 1997 Asian crisis.

quiz.q: China became a WTO member in:
In February 2026, the US Supreme Court in Learning Resources v. Trump held that:
o: The WTO has jurisdiction over US tariffs
Tariffs can be imposed freely by the president
IEEPA does not authorise the president to impose tariffs
quiz.w: The Court ruled 6-3 on 20 February 2026 that IEEPA does not authorise tariffs.

quiz.q: India's major economic liberalisation began under:
quiz.w: The 1991 balance-of-payments crisis led to LPG reforms under Rao and Manmohan Singh.
